clue.text: Pay twice when rep cut short cryptic greeting

indicators.note: something cut short loses its tail end, so the final letter goes
something cryptic is obscure and jumbled, so the letters come in a disguised order

parts.note: the word taken as written, two copies
taken as written
the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: A sales rep, laid off early, sends a puzzling note about being paid double.
explanation.walkthrough: Two copies of PAY, then WHEN and RE, rearranged give HAPPY NEW YEAR; the puzzle appeared at the turn of the year.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the standard salutation exchanged on the first of January, so it is a seasonal salutation.

clue.text: Dissident in this position almost opposite of cross?

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: here means at this place
a tick is the opposite of a cross on a marked answer; drop its last letter

explanation.surface: A rebel stands in a spot that is nearly the reverse of being angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry, but it is the X mark on a test paper, whose opposite is a tick.
explanation.definitionFit: A heretic holds opinions against accepted doctrine, just as a dissident rejects official belief.

clue.text: As leaving typical pensioner, stay

parts.note: the plural of the letter A: every A goes

indicators.note: whatever is leaving departs, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: par is the normal or average standard
OAP is old-age pensioner

explanation.surface: An elderly person stays put while others leave.
explanation.walkthrough: PAR and OAP make PAROAP; 'As' is the plural of the letter A, and taking out both As leaves PROP.
explanation.definitionFit: A stay is a support or brace holding something up, which is what a prop does.

clue.text: Artist's son took toy over? Not to start!

indicators.note: refusing to start means each word loses its opening letter and keeps the rest
turning something over flips it, so the string is read backwards

parts.note: without its first letter
without its first letter
without its first letter

explanation.surface: A painter's boy grabs a plaything and is told off for beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: Behead each of the three words, then read the string backwards. The 's is a link: the artist is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Yoko Ono is a Japanese conceptual artist and musician, widow of John Lennon.

clue.text: Doctor learnt to go around hospital entrance

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with or falsify, so the letters are altered
going around something encircles it, so one piece wraps another

parts.note: its letters rearranged
H is the map abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: A physician has studied how to get round the hospital's front door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entrance' reads as a doorway but is the verb, stressed on the second syllable; 'Doctor' is not a person but the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrance is to captivate or hold spellbound, the same as to enthral.

clue.text: Something beastly about "New New Yorker"?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the animal goes around the letter

parts.note: a yak is a beast, an animal
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: An animal story about a newcomer to New York.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'New' is the abbreviation, the rest is the definition; a Yank is also a New York Yankees baseball player.
explanation.definitionFit: Yank is slang for an American, especially a northerner, and the Yankees are New York's baseball team.

clue.text: Stripping off, Salah adds wink for show

indicators.note: stripping off takes away the outer layers, so only the inner letters remain

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters
the word without its first and last letters
the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Footballer Mohamed Salah takes his shirt off and winks for the cameras.
explanation.walkthrough: Mo Salah is a Liverpool footballer; his name supplies only its middle letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Aladdin is a favourite British Christmas pantomime, a stage production staged every winter season.

clue.text: Funny man in comic duo is out of touch

indicators.note: funny can mean odd or peculiar, so the letters are put in a strange order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The joker in a double act has lost contact with reality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny man' reads as the comedian, but 'Funny' is the signal and 'man' is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Being incommunicado means unable or unwilling to be contacted by anyone.

clue.text: A qualification?

parts.note: surface reading: any one certificate or diploma
setter's reading: the letter A names an English school exam taken at eighteen

explanation.walkthrough: The 'A' looks like the article, but A-levels are the English exams taken at the end of school, and the A stands for this phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The full name of the A-level, the school-leaving examination in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

clue.text: Right to visit apparently unpopulated part of the country

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone's place, so this letter enters the other piece

parts.note: no folk, nobody living there
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A walker claims the right to roam an empty stretch of countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apparently' flags a whimsical reading of the county name as if nobody lived there; Norfolk is a rural county in eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: Norfolk is an English county, a region or division of the nation.

clue.text: In Bow, tricky to go after vehicle? Mug!

parts.note: a tank is an armoured vehicle
hard as spoken in Cockney, which drops the H

explanation.surface: In an East End street, someone struggles to park behind a car and is called a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: Bow is in London's East End, where Cockneys drop the initial H, so hard becomes 'ard. 'Mug' looks like a fool but is the drinking vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: A tankard is a large beer drinking vessel with a handle, often pewter.

clue.text: Curse at gracious hosts

indicators.note: a host takes guests in, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: 'Gracious!' is an exclamation of surprise, like oh
taken as written

explanation.surface: Swearing at polite people who entertain guests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gracious' looks like an adjective describing the hosts, but it is the exclamation 'Gracious!'.
explanation.definitionFit: An oath can be a profane swear word, so it is a synonym of a curse.

clue.text: When all undressed, show earl odd collection

indicators.note: undressing removes the outside layers, so each word keeps only its inside

parts.note: without its first and last letters
without its first and last letters
without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A naked nobleman puts on a strange display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' looks like an adjective but is just the third word to strip; the indicator comes first, the definition last.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoard is a stash or accumulated store of valuables or goods kept together.

clue.text: Putt hit with this feeling could display aptitude

indicators.note: the combined letters, rearranged, could show a different word
the answer is what must go with the other piece, so it is what remains when that piece is taken away

parts.note: taken as written: the full set of letters
taken as written: the letters to remove

explanation.surface: A golfer with the right touch on a putt shows a natural gift.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: PUTT plus the answer rearranges to APTITUDE, so remove P, U, T, T from APTITUDE and what is left is IDEA.
explanation.definitionFit: An idea can be a vague sense or impression, as in 'I had a feeling' meaning a notion.

clue.text: Howl? The compiler? For Spooner? Possibly!

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the initial sounds trade places

parts.note: to bay is to howl like a hound; it takes the other word's opening sound
the setter refers to themselves as me; it takes the other word's opening sound

explanation.surface: A crossword setter wonders whether to howl at their own puzzle.
explanation.walkthrough: BAY ME with the opening sounds swapped becomes MAY BE. The compiler is a crossword convention for the setter, giving ME or I.
explanation.definitionFit: Maybe is an adverb meaning perhaps, expressing uncertainty.

clue.text: My son, spurning love, inspires contempt

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so one piece takes another inside

parts.note: the word minus O

indicators.note: to spurn is to reject, so that letter is thrown out

parts.note: 'Cor!' and 'My!' are both exclamations of surprise
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A parent laments that their boy, rejecting romance, provokes disdain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' looks like the possessive but is the exclamation, matched by the British 'Cor!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Scorn is a feeling of disdain towards something worthless, a synonym of contempt.

clue.text: Intend to purchase copies initially of construction materials?

indicators.note: purchase can mean grip or hold, so one piece holds another

parts.note: to mean is to intend
cc is carbon copies

indicators.note: initially points to the start, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: A builder plans to buy duplicates of the supplies first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Purchase' looks like buying but means a grip; Meccano is a metal model-building toy.
explanation.definitionFit: Meccano is a kit of metal strips, nuts and bolts for building models, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Economical aircon installed by Colin Moulding

indicators.note: something installed is fitted inside, so one piece is placed within another
moulding reshapes material, so the letters are formed into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
AC is air conditioning

explanation.surface: A tradesman called Colin fits a cheap air-conditioning unit.
explanation.walkthrough: Colin Moulding was the bassist of the band XTC, a nice disguise for the anagram signal. 'Economical' means sparing with words here.
explanation.definitionFit: Laconic speech uses very few words, and economical can mean thrifty with language.

clue.text: Somebody incompetent?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a person of importance
second meaning: split as two words, lacking capability

explanation.walkthrough: The two readings need different word splits: one word for a celebrity, two words (NOT ABLE) for the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A notable is a famous person, a somebody; read as two words it means lacking skill.

clue.text: Beat this when acquitted, and finally try treatment

parts.note: a defendant who escapes conviction is said to beat the rap

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: last letter

explanation.surface: Someone cleared in court follows up with some counselling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beat the rap' is an idiom for escaping a criminal charge, so 'this' is THE RAP.
explanation.definitionFit: Therapy is remedial care for an illness or disorder, a form of medical help.

clue.text: Rubbish solution for irritated viewers

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a lotion for sore eyes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Viewers' sounds like a TV audience annoyed by a programme, but here viewers are eyes.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both nonsense or humbug and a liquid used to bathe sore eyes.

clue.text: Fish served with dock leaves

parts.note: the gar is a long-snouted fish
to dock a ship is to land it

explanation.surface: A fish dish arrives garnished with dock leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: Dock leaves are the weed rubbed on nettle stings, but 'dock' is a verb here and 'leaves' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A garland is a wreath woven from foliage and flowers, so it is made of leaves.

clue.text: Monster improvising when cycling

indicators.note: cycling goes round in a loop, so the last letter moves round to the front

parts.note: riffing is improvising, as musicians or comics do

explanation.surface: A beast of a performer makes things up while out on a bike.
explanation.walkthrough: Move the final G of RIFFING to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A griffin is a mythical beast with an eagle's head and lion's body.

clue.text: Pupil finally in time with support for school subject

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so this letter goes within the other piece

parts.note: an age is a long period of time

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the last letter is kept

parts.note: last letter
a bra is a supporting undergarment

explanation.surface: A student arrives on time with backing for a lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' is a common crossword cue for the undergarment BRA; 'Pupil' here gives only its final letter, not a word for a student.
explanation.definitionFit: Algebra is a branch of mathematics taught in schools, a classroom discipline.

clue.text: Hands clapped themselves?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: workers, especially on a ship
second meaning: an old past tense of crow, to boast or applaud oneself

explanation.surface: Workers give themselves a round of applause.
explanation.walkthrough: To crow is to boast, to applaud yourself, and its old past tense is crew, as in 'the cock crew'.
explanation.definitionFit: Hands are sailors or workers collectively; crew is also the archaic past of crow, to brag.

clue.text: I invested in old Labour MP's land

indicators.note: money invested in something is put into it, so the letter goes inside

parts.note: Tony Benn was a veteran left-wing Labour MP
taken as written

explanation.surface: A speaker has put money into a former Labour politician's estate.
explanation.walkthrough: Tony Benn was a prominent British Labour politician who died in 2014.
explanation.definitionFit: Benin is a West African country, a nation or land beside Nigeria.

clue.text: Fit in extra guest

indicators.note: in means contained within, so the letters sit inside the following words

parts.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Squeezing one more visitor into the party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit in' looks like a phrasal verb, but 'Fit' is the definition and 'in' the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An ague is a fever with shivering bouts, so it is a fit or attack of illness.

clue.text: United in funny old game

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so this letter goes within the other piece
funny can mean odd or peculiar, so the letters are put in a strange order

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for United in team names
its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A football team stuck in a strange, outdated match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Funny old game' is a football cliché; 'old' is the fodder, not part of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Ludo is a simple board game played with dice and counters.

clue.text: River Don

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the river flowing through Durham and Sunderland
second meaning: to put on clothes

explanation.walkthrough: The Don is itself an English river, which tempts the solver to read the clue as one name; the Wear is a river in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: The Wear is an English river, and to don a garment is to put it on and wear it.

clue.text: Count drivers in some French city

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so these letters go within the other piece

parts.note: du is French for some, as in du pain
the RAC is the Royal Automobile Club, a British motoring organisation
LA is Los Angeles

explanation.surface: Tallying motorists in a city somewhere in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Count' looks like a verb, but it is the title of Bram Stoker's vampire nobleman.
explanation.definitionFit: Count Dracula is the vampire aristocrat of Bram Stoker's novel, so he is the Count.

clue.text: Perhaps tip drink over in expression of disgust

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so these letters go within the other piece

parts.note: 'Fie!' is an old cry of disgust

indicators.note: knocking a glass over turns it upside down, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: beer is a drink

explanation.surface: Someone knocks over a drink and everyone groans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip' looks like a verb to spill, but it is a gratuity, an example of a gift; 'Perhaps' flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip is money given for nothing in return, which is one example of a giveaway.

clue.text: Feeling sick in the head?

parts.note: surface reading: having a headache or a nauseous head
setter's reading: the illness exists only in the mind

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a headache; the setter means imagining you are ill, the sickness being all in the mind.
explanation.definitionFit: The condition is an excessive, unfounded worry about having a serious illness.
